headline: China Gets First Economic Scorecard With Stimulus Taps Turned On
author: Bloomberg News

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- China's economy is entering the crucial final stretch before policymakers meet next month, with its momentum again at risk of fading.
Most Read from Bloomberg

A batch of official figures due Monday will show slower increases in industrial output and consumption in October, according to the median estimates of economists surveyed by Bloomberg News. The slump in investment likely eased marginally.

The data will offer an early read on the health of the world's second-biggest economy after China stepped up efforts to bolster it in late September, deploying a quasi-fiscal program to expand investment alongside a mini-stimulus package. Top leaders are probably watching closely how growth has fared since then as they prepare for a key gathering that will set the tone for economic policy in 2027.

"The fourth quarter will be a window to gauge policy traction, whose effectiveness will partly shape next year's economic targets and the design of counter-cyclical measures," Zhang Yu, chief economist with Huachuang Securities Co., wrote in a note.
The Central Economic Work Conference usually takes place in the first half of December and offers clues about policy priorities for the following year.

When the economy rebounded in the third quarter to reach the lower end of Beijing's annual target of 4.5%-5%, net exports contributed almost 40% to the overall gain in gross domestic product — the most for any quarter since the start of 2025.

But now, concern over the sustainability of the global AI buildout are starting to call into question China's reliance on sales abroad. A less upbeat outlook for exports would put pressure on domestic demand to make up for any loss of momentum overseas.
Here's what to expect when the National Bureau of Statistics publishes the data at 10 a.m. on Monday:
Industrial output grew 5.3% last month from a year earlier, according to the median projection of economists in the Bloomberg survey, in what would be its first deceleration in three months.

The official manufacturing purchasing managers' index for October, published less than two weeks ago, already signaled a worse-than-forecast contraction in factory activity. The drop suggested a "broad-based slowdown" in the economy, said Australia & New Zealand Banking Group economists including Raymond Yeung, with a deterioration in new export orders flashing a warning sign about the resilience of demand driven by artificial intelligence.

Should the AI boom falter, it would add to risks already facing Chinese exports, ranging from higher interest rates overseas to mounting trade frictions. Weaker foreign demand may pressure Beijing to step up efforts to revive domestic household and corporate spending, after it navigated the year without bold supportive measures.
Economists polled by Bloomberg predict retail sales growth decelerated to 0.8% last month from 1.1% in September.

While autumn is typically a busy sales season, deliveries of passenger vehicles in October plunged 27% on year, according to figures provided by the China Passenger Car Association. It was the 13th straight month of their decline, as buyers become less receptive to incentives after the government scaled back subsidies, which front-loaded demand in the prior two years.

Spending by Chinese tourists during last month's Golden Week break — one of the nation's major public holidays — also dropped from levels seen in the previous two years, in another sign of sluggish consumer confidence.

With the yearslong property downturn sapping household finances, the government rolled out mortgage subsidies for qualified home buyers last month. Yet the impact of the policy will likely be limited, and authorities have indicated no plan for more forceful policies to turn the housing market around.
Fixed-asset investment is heading for a decline forecast at 7% in the first 10 months of the year, versus a 7.2% drop in January-September.

Help likely arrived from China's new financing tool that unlocked 800 billion yuan ($120 billion) in funding from state-owned policy banks. The money was deployed by Oct. 28 — less than two months after its first tranche was disbursed — as part of a program that prioritizes spending toward major national projects such as the Six Networks infrastructure initiative.
Separately, local governments were granted an additional 250 billion yuan in special bond quota last month, to be used for investment by the end of the year.

Were top leaders to conclude that additional support is needed, fiscal policy would likely lead the push, given China's central bank has telegraphed caution about cutting rates at a time when borrowing demand is anemic.

Loan and mortgage rates fell to around 3% at the end of September, lower than the levels in the US during the pandemic in 2020, when the Federal Reserve cut rates to help the economy, according to a monetary policy report published by the People's Bank of China on Wednesday.
"We expect policy focus for the rest of the year to lie in delivering results from existing measures," said Citic Securities Co. analysts led by Yang Fan in a Thursday note.
"That said, the recovery in domestic demand remains fragile, leaving room for rate cuts — particularly if export growth slows sharply."
